question: What conflicting experiences do maintainers and users report about running Bun in production, and which concrete compatibility or reliability claims can be traced to evidence rather than opinion?

claims.text: Bun maintainers said Bun 1.0 was stable and production-ready for macOS and Linux, while Windows was still highly experimental.
acceptable_patterns: Bun 1\.0 .*stable and production-ready.*macOS and Linux.*Windows .*highly experimental

evidence_passages.text: Maintainers explicitly said on September 8, 2023 that Bun 1.0 was "stable and production-ready" for macOS and Linux, while Windows was still "highly experimental" and had the package manager, test runner, and bundler disabled. https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.0

claims.text: Bun maintainers also say Node.js compatibility is still incomplete and ongoing.

evidence_passages.text: Maintainers also still say compatibility is incomplete: the docs call Node.js compatibility an "ongoing effort," and the Bun 1.4 release notes say Bun is "not 100% compatible with Node.js yet." https://bun.sh/docs, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4, https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat

claims.text: Bun documents concrete compatibility limits that can matter in production, including unimplemented `node:sea`, missing `Request` options, and lifecycle scripts being blocked by default unless trusted or allow-listed.
acceptable_patterns: lifecycle scripts are blocked by default

evidence_passages.text: Maintainers also document concrete compatibility limits that can matter in production: `node:sea` is not implemented, Bun’s `Request` support is missing `keepalive` and `duplex`, and lifecycle scripts are blocked by default except for allow-listed or explicitly trusted packages. https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat, https://bun.com/docs/pm/lifecycle

claims.text: The supplied evidence supports both successful production use and production pain, but does not support the extreme claims that Bun is broadly proven everywhere or unusable in production.
acceptable_patterns: does not support the strongest version of either side
not support .*broadly proven everywhere.*unusable in production

evidence_passages.text: The conflict is real: Bun’s maintainers market it as production-ready on macOS/Linux and point to named production adopters, while multiple users report crashes, memory leaks, missing compatibility, and cases where they still keep Node in production or as a fallback. The evidence supports both of these narrower statements, but it does **not** support the strongest version of either side ("Bun is broadly proven everywhere" or "Bun is unusable in production").

rejected_claims.text: Bun is broadly proven everywhere in production.
rejected_claims.reason: Overly broad; the supplied evidence explicitly says it does not support that strongest version.
Contradicted by supplied evidence of named production adopters and explicit note that this strongest version is not supported.

rejected_claims.text: GitHub issue reports prove how common Bun production failures are.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported by the supplied evidence; the evidence discusses concrete reports, not prevalence.
Contradicted by supplied evidence saying compatibility is an ongoing effort and Bun is not 100% compatible with Node.js yet.

rejected_claims.text: Maintainers publicly point to named production use cases for Bun, including Claude Code, Midjourney notifications, and Railway Functions.
rejected_claims.reason: The specific homepage adopter claims (Claude Code as a Bun executable, Midjourney routing every image notification through Bun's WebSocket server, Railway Functions built on Bun) trace only to the Codex run's own answer text; that run opened no URLs, so bun.com/ content was never retrieved. The second teacher run independently flags the Midjourney assertion as coming 'only from a search summary without a citable first-party statement — treat as unverified.' Beyond the sourcing gap, all three acceptable_patterns are full verbatim marketing sentences with no compositional wildcards, so a correct independent answer citing the same adopters in different words would fail grading. Unverified vendor-marketing specifics plus verbatim-only patterns.

rejected_claims.text: Users also report production problems with Bun, including crashes, memory leaks, missing compatibility, and cases where they still keep Node in production or as a fallback.
rejected_claims.reason: The substance is well corroborated (the Claude run confirms memory-leak reports in issues #24216 and #25948, a production segfault in #31159, press coverage of developer leak complaints, and the maintainers' own Rust-rewrite post conceding use-after-free/double-free defects), but the grading patterns are unusable: both are verbatim sentences of the drafting model's editorial prose ('users report crashes, memory leaks, missing compatibility, and cases where they still keep Node in production or as a fallback' / 'production workloads still surface bugs serious enough to require Node fallback'), not source language a correct answer would reproduce. Compounding this, the claim's per-source attributions rest on issues 19930/20912 and discussions 3955/17485, none of which were retrieved in either run. Rejected for overly narrow lexical patterns over unretrieved per-source attributions, not for the underlying idea, which is preserved in claim_no_support_for_extremes.
